questions.title: Question 1: Generics and the lecture's GenTest (12 marks)
questions.prompt: (a) Define generics and state four advantages. (b) For `class GenTest<T> { private T obj; void modify(T obj) { this.obj = obj; } T get() { return obj; } }`, state how many times `T` occurs and what each occurrence is. (c) Read `GenTest<Integer> a = new GenTest<Integer>();` aloud and say what `a.modify(17)` and `a.get()` accept and return. (12 marks)

steps.title: Part (a)
steps.body: Generics are an OOP concept that refers to parameterised types: a single class, method or interface works with different types of objects, so the implementation is independent of the class type. Advantages: code reuse; type safety; no need for type casting; errors are caught at compile time rather than at run time. (5 marks)

steps.title: Part (b)
steps.body: `T` occurs four times: in the class header (`GenTest<T>`, one type parameter called `T`), as the type of the instance variable `obj`, as the type of the parameter of `modify`, and as the return type of `get`. (4 marks)

steps.title: Part (c)
steps.body: "GenTest of Integer". `modify` accepts an `Integer` (so `17` is boxed) and `get` returns an `Integer`, so no cast is needed. (3 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** Four occurrences of `T`; `GenTest<Integer>` stores and returns only `Integer`.

questions.title: Question 2: Which statements compile? (12 marks)
questions.prompt: Given `GenTest<T>` as in question 1 and `Nums<T extends Number>`, say which of these compile and give the reason for each that does not: (1) `GenTest<String> a = new GenTest<String>();` (2) `GenTest<Integer> b = new GenTest<Integer>(); b.modify("CSI247");` (3) `GenTest<double> c = new GenTest<double>();` (4) `GenTest<Integer> d = new GenTest<String>();` (5) `Nums<Integer> e = new Nums<Integer>(5);` (6) `Nums<String> f = new Nums<String>("Hello");` (12 marks)

steps.title: Statements (1) and (5)
steps.body: Both compile: (1) is a `GenTest` of `String`; (5) uses `Integer`, which extends `Number`, and `5` is boxed. (4 marks)

steps.title: Statements (2) and (3)
steps.body: (2) does not compile: `incompatible types: String cannot be converted to Integer`, because `b` stores only `Integer`. (3) does not compile: `unexpected type`, because only reference types are allowed in the angle brackets (use `Double`). (4 marks)

steps.title: Statements (4) and (6)
steps.body: (4) does not compile: `incompatible types: GenTest<String> cannot be converted to GenTest<Integer>`, because the types on both sides of `=` must be identical. (6) does not compile: `type argument String is not within bounds of type-variable T`, because `String` does not extend `Number`. (4 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** (1) and (5) compile; (2), (3), (4) and (6) do not.

questions.title: Question 3: A generic class and a bounded class (14 marks)
questions.prompt: (a) Write a generic class `Box<T>` with a setter, a getter and `isEmpty()`. (b) Write `NumberBox<T extends Number>` with a method `isPositive()`. (c) Create a `Box` of `Integer`, a `Box` of `String` and a `NumberBox` of `Double`, and say why `NumberBox<String>` is rejected. (14 marks)

steps.title: Part (a)
steps.body: `public class Box<T> { private T value; public void set(T value) { this.value = value; } public T get() { return value; } public boolean isEmpty() { return value == null; } }`. (4 marks)

steps.title: Part (b)
steps.body: `public class NumberBox<T extends Number> { private T value; public NumberBox(T value) { this.value = value; } public boolean isPositive() { return value.doubleValue() > 0; } }`. The bound is what allows `doubleValue()`. (4 marks)

steps.title: Part (c)
steps.body: `Box<Integer> a = new Box<Integer>(); a.set(17);` `Box<String> b = new Box<String>(); b.set("Kago");` `NumberBox<Double> c = new NumberBox<Double>(-2.5);`. `NumberBox<String>` is rejected: `type argument String is not within bounds of type-variable T`, since `String` is not a `Number`. (6 marks)

questions.answer: **Check.** `a.get() * 2` is 34 with no cast; `b.get().toUpperCase()` is `KAGO`; `c.isPositive()` is `false`.

questions.title: Question 4: Generic methods (12 marks)
questions.prompt: Write a generic method `printArray` that prints the elements of any array of objects on one line. Call it with an `Integer` array, a `Double` array, and arrays of `Character`, `String` and `Float`. What happens with an `int` array? (12 marks)

steps.title: The method
steps.body: `public static <E> void printArray(E[] elements) { for (E element : elements) { System.out.printf("%s ", element); } System.out.println(); }`. The type parameter `<E>` goes before the return type. (5 marks)

steps.title: The calls
steps.body: One definition serves every call: `Integer[]` prints `2 4 5 7 8`, `Double[]` prints `1.0 1.5 2.5 3.5`, and a `Character[]` of the letters of Kago, a `String[]` of names and a `Float[]` print their elements in the same way. (4 marks)

steps.title: An int array
steps.body: `printArray(new int[] {1, 2})` does not compile: `method printArray cannot be applied to given types` (required `E[]`, found `int[]`), because `E` must be a reference type. Use an `Integer[]`. (3 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** One generic method prints arrays of any reference type; an array of a primitive type is rejected.

questions.title: Question 5: The Lab 7 Set (14 marks)
questions.prompt: Describe the generic class `Set<T>` of Lab 7: how the array is created and why, how `add`, `remove` and `search` work, and the cells of a `Set<Integer>` after `add(7)`, `add(12)`, `add(7)`, `remove(7)` and `add(5)`. (14 marks)

steps.title: The array
steps.body: An array of 10 cells of type `T`, all `null` at first. `new T[10]` is not allowed (`generic array creation`), so the constructor creates `(T[]) new Object[10]`, an unchecked cast that is marked `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")`. (4 marks)

steps.title: The operations
steps.body: `add(T t)` stores the element in the first empty cell (duplicates are allowed). `remove(T t)` finds the first element for which `equals` is true and sets its cell to `null`. `search(T t)` returns the first element equal to `t` (by `equals`), or `null`. (5 marks)

steps.title: The cells
steps.body: After `add(7)`, `add(12)`, `add(7)`: 7, 12, 7. After `remove(7)`: empty, 12, 7 (the first 7 is removed). After `add(5)`: 5, 12, 7, because the first empty cell is cell 0 again. (5 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** Cells 0 to 2 are 5, 12, 7 and the other seven cells are empty. `search(12)` returns 12 and `search(99)` returns `null`.

questions.title: Question 6: Generic interfaces and bounds (12 marks)
questions.prompt: (a) Write a generic interface `BigAndSmall<T extends Comparable<T>>` with `small()` and `big()`, and a generic class `Range<T>` that implements it for an array of `T`. (b) Say what happens with `class G implements BigAndSmall<T>` when `T` is not declared. (c) Give `small()` and `big()` for the `Integer` values 42, 7, 19, 63. (12 marks)

steps.title: Part (a)
steps.body: `public interface BigAndSmall<T extends Comparable<T>> { T small(); T big(); }` and `public class Range<T extends Comparable<T>> implements BigAndSmall<T>` holding a `T[]`, whose `small()` and `big()` loop through the array and compare with `compareTo`. The bound is what makes `compareTo` available. (6 marks)

steps.title: Part (b)
steps.body: It does not compile: `cannot find symbol` (symbol: class `T`). The implementing class must declare the type parameter (`class G<T extends Comparable<T>> implements BigAndSmall<T>`), that is, it must be generic. (3 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** The bound gives `compareTo`; the class must be generic; smallest 7, biggest 63.
